title: Why is the SRD grant stuck at R370?

scenes.label: every month
lines: Three hundred and seventy rand.
That's what about eight million South Africans get every month from the SRD grant.
Six years ago it was three hundred and fifty rand.
Since then, bread, taxi fares and electricity have all gone up. The grant barely moved.
So why is it stuck? And what can you actually do about it? Let's open the case.

scenes.headline: The R370 Grant
scenes.sub: Why it's stuck, and what you can do
lines: Case file: the R370 grant.
The grant started in 2020, during the Covid lockdown.
Millions of people lost their income overnight, so government created a temporary three hundred and fifty rand payment.
It was meant to last a few months.
Instead, it has been extended every single year since then.
In 2024 it went up by twenty rand, to three hundred and seventy. That's the only increase it has ever had.
And in February this year, government extended it again, at the same amount, until the end of March 2027.
Today, about eight and a half million people are paid each month.
But around fifteen million people are on the system.
To qualify, the money coming into your account must be less than six hundred and twenty four rand a month.
Earn a little more than that, and you're out.

scenes.headline: Three reasons it's stuck

cards.title: Money
cards.sub: Treasury says it can't afford more

cards.title: "Temporary"
cards.sub: No law, renewed one year at a time

lines: So why hasn't it grown? There are three main suspects.
Money. The word temporary. And prices.

scenes.headline: What it costs each year
lines: Suspect number one: money.
The grant costs about forty billion rand a year.
In court, Treasury said making it bigger, and raising the income limit, could cost up to one hundred and thirty nine billion rand a year.
Treasury says government simply can't afford that right now.
But the activists who took government to court point out that the twenty rand increase in 2024 cost only about two billion rand.
So small, regular increases are possible. It's a choice about priorities.

scenes.headline: Renewed one year at a time
scenes.quote: It will still be a temporary provision until such time that there is a law.
lines: Suspect number two: the word temporary.
The SRD grant is not in any law. It lives in short-term rules that must be renewed every year.
Because it's always temporary, nobody plans a proper increase.
Government says it is working on a permanent replacement, a grant linked to jobs, skills and small business.
But the minister told Parliament that making a new policy takes about five years on average.
Until that law exists, the department says, the SRD will stay a temporary payment.

scenes.headline: Grant vs. a basic food list
scenes.note: Cash-out fees at some shops: about R10 per R100
lines: Suspect number three: prices.
In March, Daily Maverick priced a list of fourteen basic food items. It came to four hundred and twenty six rand.
That's fifty six rand more than the whole grant.
And if you withdraw your money at a spaza or shop, fees can take about ten rand for every hundred.
Every year the grant stays frozen, it buys a little less.

steps.title: Government appeals
steps.text: Says it can't afford the changes

lines: There's also a court case that could change everything.
In January 2025, the Pretoria High Court found that parts of the SRD rules are unconstitutional.
It said people must be allowed to apply in person, not only online. It said the income limit and the grant must go up over time. And it said once-off gifts shouldn't count as income.
Government appealed.
The Supreme Court of Appeal heard the case on the twenty fifth of August. The judges have not decided yet.

scenes.headline: The monthly bank check
lines: That last point matters, because of how SASSA checks you.
Every month, SASSA looks at the money coming into your bank account.
If your sister sends you three hundred rand, a relative helps with school shoes, and your stokvel pays out, that can add up to more than six hundred and twenty four rand.
The system can count it as income, and you're declined for that month.
The Institute for Economic Justice says most rejections come from this money check, and many of them are wrong.

scenes.headline: Stuck by design
points: Waiting on the courts and a new law
lines: So, the verdict.
The grant is stuck because it was built as a temporary fix, the budget is tight, and its permanent replacement isn't ready.
The courts and a new law could still change that. But that will take time.

items.title: Declined? Read the reason
items.sub: Then appeal if it's wrong. Don't wait

items.title: Keep your details up to date
Never pay or share your PIN
items.sub: SASSA will never ask for it

lines: So what can you do right now?
One. Check your status every month, and only on the official site, s r d dot sassa dot gov dot za.
Two. If you're declined, read the reason. If it's wrong, like a gift counted as income, appeal. There is a time limit, so don't wait.
Three. Keep your phone number and bank details up to date, or your payment can get stuck.
Four. Watch the fees. Compare where you withdraw, so more of the three seventy stays in your pocket.
And five. Never pay anyone to apply, and never share your PIN. SASSA will never ask for it.

scenes.headline: Case still open
lines: This case is still open. When the court decides, we'll explain what it means for you.
